item.title: Teaching Intermolecular Forces through a Watercolor Painting Activity
item.description:
Abstract This Activity discusses the development and implementation of an art-based activity to teach intermolecular forces (IMFs). A watercolor laboratory activity was developed in which students identified the IMFs within various art materials and the IMFs present between different molecules and ions. The students observed how these materials interact while painting with watercolors. This activity was conducted in a nonmajor, art-focused chemistry course and in a general-chemistry course. Pretest, post-tests, and laboratory reports show that the activity helped students identify IMFs, the students enjoyed the activity, and the students felt the activity helped them better understand IMFs in both the nonmajor, art-focused chemistry course and the general chemistry course.

item.title: Instructional Interventions for Acid–Base Concepts in Chemistry Education: A Meta-Analysis of Achievement Outcomes
item.description:
Abstract This meta-analysis examined the effects of instructional interventions on students’ academic achievement in acid–base chemistry. Searches were conducted in Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, ULAKBİM TR Index, the Turkish National Thesis Center, EBSCOhost, and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global using terms related to acid–base concepts, achievement, and learning outcomes. Google Scholar was also used as a supplementary source. The final sample comprised 69 studies: 38 articles, 23 master’s theses, seven doctoral dissertations, and one conference paper. Across these studies, intervention groups achieved higher scores than control or comparison groups, with a very large overall effect (Hedges’ g = 1.160, 95% CI [0.982, 1.339]). However, substantial heterogeneity and a prediction interval that included zero indicated considerable variation in effect sizes across studies. Neither instructional intervention type nor educational level showed significant differences in effect size, and intervention duration was not a significant predictor. Thus, the results do not support the consistent superiority of any broad instructional approach. Future research should therefore look beyond broad intervention labels and examine more closely how instructional approaches are implemented and aligned with learning objectives. item.title: Integrating Theory and Practice: An Instrument-DIY Approach to Biochemistry Education
item.description:
Abstract As an interdisciplinary course, biochemistry objectives should encompass competency-based goals such as the ability to innovate experimental techniques for solving practical problems. Understanding the operation principles of important biochemical techniques as well as instruments is crucial to promote students’ interest, critical thinking, and innovation. Therefore, we developed an ″Instrument-DIY″ module that integrates theory and practice within our integrative biochemistry course. In this approach, the lecture classes cover the fundamental principles including background introduction, structure, and wiring design, through DIY installation of a chemiluminescence imager as a case study. The laboratory classes then focus on instrument building and testing, allowing students to apply theoretical concepts in a hands-on manner. Through a comparison of classes with (N = 64) and without (N = 67) the ″Instrument-DIY″ module, the hands-on DIY experience has been shown to enhance student engagement and motivation, thereby leading to improved academic performance and demonstrating how theoretical knowledge can be effectively translated into practical applications. Furthermore, the self-built imager also serves as a valuable resource to assist National College Student Innovation and Entrepreneurship Training Program (NCSIE) projects and academic competitions.

item.title: StereoMatch: A Card Game Designed for Teaching and Learning Stereochemical Relationships of Organic Compounds
item.description:
Abstract Stereochemistry is an essential learning objective in introductory organic chemistry and is applicable to numerous advanced topics. Although gamification is an effective teaching tool to enhance the learning experience of various concepts in organic chemistry, gamifying the identification of stereoisomers has not been developed extensively. Herein, we report StereoMatch, a simple and accessible card game designed for teaching and learning stereochemical relationships of organic molecules in sophomore organic chemistry courses (in-person or virtually). Inspired by Set, the game rule centers on players or teams being able to match cards according to the stereochemical relationships between the cards shown. StereoMatch can be used as an in-class activity or a study tool for an exam review session for organic chemistry courses. The card game provides a collaborative environment where students and teachers can be interactive and make learning stereochemical concepts fun. Our demonstration of StereoMatch with Clemson University students and our analysis of pre- and postgame surveys/quizzes revealed that a majority of students not only improved their confidence and knowledge on identifying various stereoisomers but also enjoyed the card game.

item.title: From Life Scenarios to Chemistry Classroom: Construction of Situational Teaching Cases for Core Chemical Concepts in Senior High School with Hainan Regional Characteristics
item.description:
Abstract Guided by constructivism and situated-cognition theories as well as the principles of scientificity, distinctiveness, and operability, this study uses Hainan’s seawater magnesium extraction and coconut-oil refining as local resources to build a five-stage case-construction model: “resource screening and analysis ─ core-concept connection ─ teaching-model design ─ case development and implementation ─ evaluation and optimization”. It demonstrates how real-life situations can be converted into instructional contexts for core high-school chemistry concepts including substance transformation and separation and purification, through hierarchical problem chains, inquiry-oriented tasks and literacy-focused extension activities. Deep integration of regional resources with chemistry disciplinary knowledge yields a replicable five-link teaching framework: “context creation ─ problem-driven inquiry ─ task-based exploration ─ transfer and application ─ literacy elevation”. An exploratory quasi-experimental design with intact grade-11 classes was adopted to preliminarily examine the instructional potential of these contextualized cases. The core contribution of this research is a transferable paradigm integrating regional characteristics and disciplinary logic for developing localized chemistry core-concept teaching cases, alongside theoretical and methodological references for regional chemistry resource construction and classroom practice.

item.title: A Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experience in Nonaqueous Redox Flow Battery Chemistry
item.description:
Abstract Teaching electrochemistry well requires conceptual understanding, practical experience with measurement and analysis, and opportunities to apply both to a real electrochemical problem. We developed a course-based undergraduate research experience (CURE) in which students investigated metal acetylacetonate complexes as candidates for nonaqueous redox flow batteries (NARFBs). Students began with a shared investigation of Fe(acac)3 before working in teams to select, prepare, characterize, and electrochemically evaluate candidate complexes. Teams used primary literature, experimental results, and practical constraints to defend a final NARFB design recommendation. Structured discussions provided opportunities to troubleshoot results and revise experimental plans as the work progressed. The project was implemented across two course offerings with 29 students. Assessment results supported learning across all eight outcomes, with the strongest evidence for research planning, integration of experimental evidence, and scientific communication. Student reflections emphasized the value of open-ended work, iteration, and ownership.

item.title: The Sound of Light: Use of Sonification for the Creation of Audiovisual Introductions to Light-Based Analytical Chemistry Methods in an Undergraduate Laboratory
item.description:
Abstract Sonification – the translation of data into nonspeech sounds – can offer possibilities to make learning more accessible to students. This study explores its use in combination with visual representation to introduce atom absorption spectrometry and photometry to undergraduate students in a laboratory course on analytical chemistry. Based on the Universal Design for Learning approach, we employed and evaluated a method that used additional modes of representation during introductions to those methods. Sonified representations were used in addition to visualization to represent light’s changing qualities regarding intensity and color on its path through the spectrometer and photometer. The materials illustrate how light interacts with key components of the analytical instruments, mapping its changing intensity to changing rhythmic patterns and its wavelength to sound pitch. Postintervention surveys (4-point Likert-scale, maximum level of 4 and open responses) of 151 students indicated high intervention attractiveness values (photometry: 3.52 ± 0.33; atom absorption spectroscopy: 3.46 ± 0.40). Open form feedback was used to improve the introduction method between implementations and allowed for analysis of student perspectives.

item.title: Integrating Innovative Assessment in Polymer Course: A Polymer Timeline Challenge of Polymer History
item.description:
Abstract Teaching the history of polymer science is often challenging because students tend to perceive historical developments as isolated facts rather than as interconnected scientific advances that shape modern materials. To address this challenge, an interactive instructional activity known as “Polymer Timeline Challenge”, was implemented in the Polymer course for Materials Engineering Programme at the International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM). The activity requires students to work collaboratively in small groups to construct digital timelines that illustrates major milestones in Polymer Science, from natural polymers to contemporary developments in smart and sustainable polymers. Using digital platforms such as Canva, Padlet, Google Slides, and Animaker, students integrated historical events, key scientists, polymer structures, processing methods, applications, and societal impacts into interactive multimedia presentations. The activity culminated in group presentations and class discussions that connected historical breakthroughs with modern challenges in sustainability, materials innovation, and engineering applications. Several groups further enhanced engagement through creative approaches, including role-play and multimedia storytelling. Instructor observations and student reflections indicated that the timeline format encouraged students to view polymer science as an evolving discipline rather than a collection of disconnected concepts. item.title: Electrochemical Production of High-Purity Hydrogen Peroxide: An Undergraduate Laboratory Experiment Using a Molecular Catalyst
item.description:
Abstract The electrochemical production of high-purity hydrogen peroxide via the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) offers a sustainable method for synthesizing this important chemical. This laboratory experiment, designed for undergraduate students, integrates fundamental chemistry, electrochemistry, and practical device fabrication knowledge. Using a molecular catalyst as a model, students explore catalyst preparation, electrochemical testing, and product quantification. The experiment covers key topics such as the mechanism of the ORR, the role of molecular catalysts, reaction pathways, and performance evaluation. Through hands-on experience in electrode fabrication and data analysis, students will develop a comprehensive understanding of how material properties influence electrochemical behavior and product yield. Students will be encouraged to critically identify sources of inefficiency and propose strategies for improving catalyst performance. By bridging theoretical knowledge with practical application, this experiment prepares students to contribute to the development of green chemistry solutions for the energy and chemical industries.

item.title: Having Students Develop Three-Dimensional Learning Assessment Tasks to Enhance Understanding and Career Readiness within an Upper-Level Elective Chemistry Course
item.description:
Abstract Years of evidence reveal that students leave our undergraduate courses with an incoherent understanding of chemistry content and are often less prepared in 21st century skills than desired. One initiative aimed to address this concern, referred to as Three-Dimensional Learning (3DL), includes reflecting on what we want students to know (core ideas), how we want students to use that knowledge (science and engineering practices - SEPs), and lenses/tools to explain a range of phenomena across disciplines (crosscutting concepts). While growing evidence supports the need to further expand this initiative within all courses, it has been primarily implemented at the K-12 and introductory undergraduate levels with little movement to upper-level courses. In this paper, the 3DL Framework was leveraged in a senior upper-level elective course for chemistry and biochemistry majors to provide students an opportunity to holistically reflect on the understanding and skills obtained within their degree program. As a final project for the course, students were tasked to create 3DL-aligned assessment questions, which required students to continually explore their own knowledge on a deeper level to explain how and why phenomena occur. The results presented in this paper highlight how students were able to refine their chemistry knowledge and better understand how the different subdisciplines are connected through core ideas. item.title: Development of a Portable 3D-Printed Fluorescence Imager for Student-Centered Learning in an Open-Lab Course
item.description:
Abstract Traditional fluorescence imagers, often bulky, expensive “black boxes”, limit student access to their internal optics and are impractical for resource-constrained educational settings. To address these pedagogical and practical barriers, we designed and fabricated a lightweight, portable fluorescence imaging device (≈300 g) integrated with a smartphone. All core components including the dark box, optical module holder, sample positioning area, and imaging area were fully 3D printed, keeping total material costs below \$40. Using fluorescent microneedle (MN) arrays as the imaging target, we optimized camera parameters and placed the MN patch in the illumination chamber. Image acquisition is typically completed within 1 min, enabling precise quantification of color and intensity. The study also evaluated the effects of ambient temperature and lighting on MN imaging. Notably, the device features an adjustable MN holder that allows imaging angles to be flexibly set between 10° and 30°. This low-cost, open-design platform provides an accessible hands-on tool for real-time fluorescence observation and analysis, making it a viable and economical option for institutions with limited equipment budgets to expand hands-on access to optical instrumentation. More importantly, the device was embedded within an inquiry-based laboratory course that engaged students in an iterative process of equipment assembly, optimization, and application. item.title: An Integrated Laboratory Module Linking Enzyme Kinetics, Inhibition, and Ligand Binding Thermodynamics Using Glutathione S-Transferase
item.description:
Abstract Enzyme inhibition is central to biochemistry and drug discovery. However, undergraduate laboratory instruction often treats enzyme kinetics, inhibition, and ligand binding as separate topics, limiting students’ ability to relate activity-based parameters to thermodynamic descriptions of molecular recognition. We report an integrated laboratory module for upper-division undergraduate courses that combines steady-state enzyme kinetics, inhibition analysis, intrinsic fluorescence spectroscopy, and isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) with glutathione S-transferase as a model enzyme. Using reduced glutathione (GSH) as the substrate and glutathione sulfonate as a competitive inhibitor, students determine Michaelis–Menten parameters, inhibition constants (Ki), and IC50 values. They also independently characterize equilibrium binding and thermodynamic parameters from spectroscopic and calorimetric data. By analyzing complementary data sets obtained under consistent experimental conditions, students compare kinetic and equilibrium constants, evaluate underlying assumptions, and relate enzyme activity with binding energetics. The module promotes quantitative data analysis, nonlinear regression, and critical interpretation of experimental models within a unified experimental framework.

item.title: Just Because You Can, Does Not Mean You (Always) Should: The Ethical Implications of Using Generative AI in Chemistry Education
item.description:
Abstract The proliferation of accessible generative AI platforms continues to accelerate in society. With this growth, educators are looking to understand how to best train their students to engage in their work and society with this new technology. Most research in this realm has focused on training students to consider when and how to use generative AI, with newer work focused on the impacts on learning. Yet, there has been little exploration of training educators and educational researchers on when and how to use generative AI. While there are some nascent ethical codes emerging, individual exploration of whether, when, and how to use AI in our role as educators deserves attention. In this manuscript, we describe three frameworks of normative ethics, namely, utilitarianism, deontology, and virtue ethics, and explore instructor use cases for generative AI. We do not intend this work to advocate for a specific stance on the use of AI but to invite the reader and our community to engage with the question of their own ethical stance in the context of their own use of the new technology.

item.title: Relationship between Chemistry Classroom Social Environment and Academic Resilience: A Cross-Sectional Moderated Serial Mediation Analysis
item.description:
Abstract Chemistry academic resilience has emerged as an important psychological resource for successful chemistry learning. However, how environmental and individual factors are associated with academic resilience remains insufficiently understood. This study examined the associations of two environmental factors─chemistry classroom social environment and perceived parental emotional warmth─and two individual factors─self-handicapping and self-regulated learning in chemistry─with chemistry academic resilience. Building on relevant theory and prior research, this study examined a theoretically specified moderated serial mediation model using cross-sectional survey data from 1503 Chinese senior high school students. Observed-variable path analysis based on composite scale scores was used to estimate direct, indirect, and conditional indirect associations. Within the specified model, the chemistry classroom social environment had a positive direct association with chemistry academic resilience (B = 0.166). At the mean level of perceived parental emotional warmth, positive indirect associations were estimated through self-handicapping in chemistry and self-regulated learning in chemistry separately (estimates = 0.052 and 0.178, respectively), as well as through their hypothesized serial arrangement (estimate = 0.039). item.title: Algorithmic Experiment Descriptions: Fostering Computational Thinking in Chemistry Class
item.description:
Abstract Students are growing up in a highly digitized world in which STEM careers rely on a variety of technologies. To provide students with a realistic view of STEM professions and prepare them adequately, relevant skills need to be addressed in school. Computational thinking (CT) is a key competence not only for applying technology but also for understanding and actively influencing it. Many CT skills are reflected in problem-solving processes within the natural sciences and can thus be fostered in interdisciplinary science lessons. However, chemistry education research does not offer a wide range of interdisciplinary approaches that foster CT, and concerns about technical issues can prevent teachers from using new technology in their classrooms. We introduce a teaching approach that addresses CT in chemistry class without technology. Using a participatory action research design, we developed and iteratively evaluated an unplugged CT intervention for secondary chemistry education in which students use flowcharts to algorithmically plan, represent, and conduct chemical experiments. By using algorithmic notation for experimental descriptions, the presented unplugged unit successfully combines the promotion of CT competencies with chemistry learning objectives. The students plan and conduct an experiment using flowcharts as notation, thereby demonstrating significant learning gains in chemistry and CT. item.title: Embedding Authentic Medicinal Chemistry Reasoning through a Virtual Lead-Optimization Activity
item.description:
Abstract Authentic learning experiences that reflect the reasoning practices of professional scientists are intended to support the development of higher-order decision-making skills. This article presents a fully virtual lead-optimization (vLO) activity designed to embed medicinal chemistry reasoning within the curriculum. Using a curated PI3Kδ inhibitor dataset and a sequence of scaffolded design stages, students analyze structure–activity relationships, evaluate multiparameter tradeoffs, and justify molecular design decisions under conditions of uncertainty. Early design stages provide full access to experimental data to support reflection and interrogation of missed opportunities, whereas a final predictive stage requires students to apply Free–Wilson reasoning to propose new analogues from predicted or calculated properties. The vLO is assessed by submission of an individual, professional-style report, describing the process, reasoning and analysis of the optimization. The vLO activity offers a scalable, research-aligned approach for developing decision-making competencies central to medicinal chemistry and provides a transferable framework for incorporating authentic, data-rich inquiry into chemistry education.

item.title: A Gamified Knight’s Tour for Teaching Metabolic Pathways
item.description:
Abstract Gamification is increasingly recognized as an effective strategy for enhancing student engagement and conceptual understanding in science education. This work introduces a classroom-tested active learning activity that uses the Knight’s Tour puzzle, a logic challenge based on the chess knight’s movement, to teach glycolysis in undergraduate biochemistry courses. Students collaborate in teams to solve grid-based puzzles that reveal hidden sentences related to enzymatic steps, regulatory mechanisms, and metabolic logic. The activity promotes motivation, problem-solving, and conceptual reinforcement, as students must connect biochemical terminology and pathway sequences while navigating the puzzle. Multiple grid formats (4 × 4, 4 × 5, and 5 × 5) were designed to embed progressively complex biochemical statements. The puzzles can be completed within typical class sessions and integrate seamlessly into lectures. Informal classroom observations indicate improved student participation, stronger retention of key biochemical concepts, and positive attitudes toward learning. The activity is highly flexible and can be adapted to other metabolic pathways or scientific topics, making it a versatile tool that supports active learning, teamwork, and deeper understanding in biochemistry.

item.title: Smartphone-Assisted Digital Image Colorimetry for the Determination of Iron Content in Spinach for High School Students
item.description:
Abstract To develop a simple, low-cost quantitative analytical approach for chemistry teaching, this study integrated smartphone-assisted digital image colorimetry (DIC) into the quantitative determination of iron content in spinach for high school education. A lightweight web tool, Concentration Determination by Image Analysis (CDIM 1.0), was developed to support the colorimetric quantification workflow. In this teaching experiment, students completed spinach iron extraction and a series of iron standard solution preparations. With a user-friendly graphical interface platform, students acquired image-based data, plotted standard calibration curves, and quantified iron concentrations in real spinach samples. The DIC detection results exhibited high consistency with traditional spectrophotometry, with a relative error of less than 5% for Fe2+ measurement. Variations in smartphone models exerted negligible impacts on experimental outcomes. This method can serve as a viable alternative to professional spectrophotometers for quantitative analysis in high school chemistry instructional scenarios. Featuring simple operation and low experimental cost, this approach is adaptable to quantitative analytical teaching in diverse secondary educational settings.

item.title: Electrochemical Detection of Ethanol in Liquid Samples and Simulated Breath: Investigating Calibration, Selectivity, and Preconcentration
item.description:
Abstract Advances in miniaturized and point-of-care electrochemical sensors have expanded their applications in healthcare, environmental monitoring, and public safety. Consequently, it is important to study the principles of these technologies in an undergraduate setting. This experiment uses screen-printed electrodes for electrochemical detection of ethanol and introduces students to electrocatalysis, calibration curves, chemical interference, selectivity, and preconcentration. Students use cyclic voltammetry and chronoamperometry to make calibration curves and determine ethanol concentrations in ethanol standards and diluted beer and wine samples. Glucose interference is investigated, and a simulated breath experiment demonstrates how selecting breath as the analytical sample and condensing it can eliminate interference while simultaneously preconcentrating ethanol. The activity provides an opportunity to discuss blood alcohol concentration, breath alcohol concentration, and modern alcohol-sensing technologies. This experiment is suitable for upper-level undergraduate courses in analytical chemistry, physical chemistry, and electrochemistry.

item.title: Simulated Scenarios for Chemistry Lab: A Smartphone-Assisted Pharmaceutical Inspector
item.description:
Abstract Traditional STEM education increasingly benefits from integrating accessible digital technologies that reflect authentic professional practice. This study presents a smartphone-based quantitative colorimetry approach implemented in simulated professional scenarios to support instrumental analysis instruction at the high school and first-year university levels through defined roles between lecturers and students. The method employs a smartphone camera and BGR and CIELAB color models for quantitative analysis, validated against conventional analytical techniques with high precision and reproducibility. The strategy is illustrated through a simulated pharmaceutical quality control scenario (n = 40), where participants assumed professional roles and compared conventional visual methods with smartphone-based analysis. This approach promoted the application of pharmacopoeial criteria, integration of qualitative and quantitative data, and development of evidence-based decision-making, collaborative work, and resource-efficient practices. Measured outcomes included 100% correct identification of an adulterated paracetamol sample using both visual comparison and digital criteria, an approximate 40% reduction in decision time with the digital method, peer evaluation scores above 4/5 in teamwork and communication, and 95% of students demonstrating the ability to justify quality control decisions in terms of public health impact. item.title: Measuring Course-Level Belonging and Perceived Social Doubt of Science Fit in General Chemistry: Instrument Development and Invariance Testing
item.description:
Abstract Sense of belonging and science identity are recognized as key predictors of success in STEM fields. However, there are limited tools available for simultaneously assessing these aspects, particularly concerning the social recognition of science fit and its relationship to belonging. Additionally, many existing instruments lack invariance testing, which is crucial for examining differences across demographic groups. To address these gaps, we present findings from both exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, as well as invariance testing, of an initial 33-question Likert-scale survey administered in General Chemistry at a midsized, research-intensive private institution in the Midwest region of the United States. The results from the exploratory factor analysis revealed a three-factor structure: measuring course-level sense of belonging (CSB), course-level belonging threat (CBT), and perceived social doubt of science fit (PSDSF). The confirmatory factor analysis indicated a good fit for the proposed model (CFI = 0.968, TLI = 0.960, RMSEA = 0.055, SRMR = 0.043), supporting the structural validity of the data. Furthermore, invariance testing confirmed the construct validity of the data across various demographic groups, including course year, binary gender, first-generation status, and program of study. item.title: An Exploratory Study on How Student Resources Interact with Prior Knowledge and Experiences to Influence Reasoning
item.description:
Abstract Students’ prior knowledge and learning experiences have been shown to impact how students reason in chemistry contexts. However, much of the previous work on students’ prior knowledge has focused on the misconceptions students have rather than exploring the utility of students’ ideas and thinking for learning chemistry. Using the resources perspective and semistructured interviews, this work explored student reasoning about Maxwell–Boltzmann frequency distributions in general chemistry II and identified five resources in which students connected to prior knowledge outside of chemistry including high temperature means high velocity, lighter and smaller means faster, faster velocity means more spread out and more space, changes in one “thing” causes changes in another, and energy as currency. These resources were connected to heavy and light objects, athletes, roller coasters, storing perfume, and other situations outside of chemistry and were employed to make sense of the frequency distributions. In this paper, we explore the context-dependent nature of these resources and how the connections students make with these resources and their prior knowledge appear to shape conclusions and inferences. We close out this paper with implications for instruction and research.

item.title: Green Chemistry Case Studies in the Classroom: Supporting Instructors with a New, Easy-to-Use Template
item.description:
Abstract A Template and User Guide for creating custom case studies has been created to assist instructors in infusing their courses with themes of green chemistry and sustainability. Case study-based teaching has a rich history across diverse fields and has been proven to enhance student learning and engagement. Moreover, the ACS Guidelines for Bachelor’s Degree Programs encourage instructors to expose students to green chemistry through real-world case studies. The template and guide presented here are designed to help instructors quickly develop their own case studies and overcome known barriers with respect to time, expertise, and curricular content. The template provides a list of suggested case study components, and the accompanying User Guide gives context and background for selecting a topic, defining clear and assessable learning objectives, and developing relevant course materials. Two examples of case studies built using these tools are provided: one suitable for general chemistry courses and one relevant to the organic chemistry curriculum. Ideally, the template and guide will facilitate the rapid development of green chemistry case studies that can be shared with other instructors to propagate and strengthen green chemistry education across higher education.

item.title: Chemistry in the Cocina Latina: A Cross-Disciplinary Approach to Enrich College Education
item.description:
Abstract We introduce a new integrative course showcasing how scientific literacy and cultural fluency are not mutually exclusive but mutually reinforcing, preparing students for leadership in an increasingly diverse world. Intercultural competence is becoming indispensable for learners across disciplines, especially within STEM fields. This cross-disciplinary course connects foundational concepts in chemistry with an introduction to the understanding of LatinX and Hispanic culture, both taught through the lens of food and cooking. We weave in the exploration of chemical processes and reactions that are inherent in all aspects of cooking with a humanistic perspective, examining how language, cultural context, and interpersonal dynamics shape every step of food preparation and enjoyment. By approaching the domain of food preparation through the lens of a physical science, we provide students with the opportunity to learn the processes of hypothesis formation, experimental design, and data analysis through tangible, real-world scenarios, while heightening awareness of the growing influence of Hispanic migrant voices in contemporary society.

item.title: High Ability Students: A Closer Look at Czech Students Excelling in Chemistry
item.description:
Abstract Despite sustained attention to high ability students in the natural sciences, this field remains theoretically and empirically open. This study focuses on Czech students identified as gifted or high ability in chemistry and contributes to a deeper understanding of giftedness in the natural sciences. Drawing on qualitative data from in-depth semistructured interviews, the findings highlight the role of teacher support, while emphasizing the importance of like-minded peers. Peer relationships appear to play a key role in mitigating the social isolation frequently experienced by high ability students. Participants described peer learning groups as a valuable source of belonging, interaction, and continued engagement with chemistry. The results contribute to a more nuanced understanding of high ability students’ motivation and offer implications for educational practices that strengthen their potential for both individual development and societal benefit.

item.title: Critical Student Assessment of AI-Generated Chemical Drawings
item.description:
Abstract This activity describes the generation and critical evaluation of AI-generated chemical drawings by sophomore chemistry majors. AI-generated chemical drawings are frequently broadly deficient with respect to framework architectures, valence exceptions, and nonsensical placements of atoms, functional groups, or double bonds. This timely and highly interactive activity is imbued with rich learning potential. It proved to be thought-provoking and delighted the students involved.

item.title: From Metal Corrosion to Energy Conversion: An Integrated Electrochemical Perspective for Undergraduate Education
item.description:
Abstract Electrochemical corrosion is a ubiquitous materials phenomenon characterized by continuous interfacial charge transfer and measurable corrosion currents, providing a direct window into reaction kinetics. In this laboratory experiment, corrosion behavior was investigated through two complementary approaches. Self-corrosion currents are quantified via Tafel extrapolation, while galvanic currents are measured in electrically coupled metal systems. Comparison of these data sets allowed evaluation of rate differences among metals and clarification of the mechanistic distinction between spontaneous single-electrode reactions and electrically coupled systems. To extend the analysis beyond electrochemical parameters, in situ optical microscopy was employed to monitor surface evolution during corrosion, and students subsequently constructed a corrosion-based Zn cell to examine time-dependent electrical output under varying pH conditions. X-ray diffraction identifies corrosion products and correlates phase formation with electrochemical response. By integrating kinetic measurement, real-time observation, energy analysis, and structural characterization, the experiment promotes quantitative reasoning and interdisciplinary understanding. The laboratory design strengthens students’ ability to interpret electrochemical data, relate electrical signals to material transformation, and connect corrosion phenomena with broader concepts in materials and energy chemistry.

item.title: Quantitative Analysis of Ethanol in Beer Using ATR-IR and Raman─An Undergraduate Lab for Instrumental Analytical Chemistry
item.description:
Abstract This undergraduate instrumental analysis experiment introduces students to the application of Raman spectroscopy and attenuated total reflectance infrared spectroscopy (ATR-IR) for the quantitative determination of ethanol in local brewery beer samples. Raman spectroscopy, coupled with an internal standard and a simple distillation procedure, allows for the selective quantification of ethanol (Boyci). In contrast, ATR-IR offers a rapid, direct, and nondestructive approach requiring minimal sample preparation. The experiment promotes an understanding of molecular vibrational techniques and provides practical insight into analytical decision-making (Dent). Ethanol standards and beer samples from a local brewery were used to contextualize the analysis within a real-world setting.

item.title: Smartphone-Based Simulated Photometer for Teaching Spectrophotometry Using AI-Assisted Tools
item.description:
Abstract This study proposes an approach that uses generative artificial intelligence (AI) to develop a web application capable of interfacing with a smartphone camera and performing quantitative RGB-based chemical measurements. Using this method, students can readily convert their own smartphones into simple photometers for immediate use in the classroom. With teacher guidance, students employ AI agents to create HTML files that activate the smartphone camera and extract RGB values from captured images, converting light intensity measurements into absorbance data. Unlike conventional commercial software, which is generally immutable and operates as a closed system, this approach enables students to develop customized simulated photometers based on their unique design concepts by manipulating AI prompt inputs. By employing this approach, students are able to rapidly configure a simulated spectrophotometer utilizing solely their smartphones within the classroom environment, without the need for any additional external equipment, thereby enabling them to perform a range of simulated spectrophotometric experiments. item.title: Mathematics Preparation, Intrinsic Motivation, Self-Efficacy, and Achievement in General Chemistry II: A Structural Equation Modeling Study
item.description:
Abstract Introductory chemistry often functions as a gateway course for students pursuing STEM majors and science-related careers. Although mathematics preparation and self-efficacy are well-established predictors of general chemistry achievement, less is known about how these factors operate together with intrinsic motivation and about which types of intrinsic motivation are most closely linked to students’ self-efficacy. Guided by social cognitive theory and self-determination theory, this study used latent-variable structural equation modeling to examine how mathematics preparation, intrinsic motivation, and self-efficacy explained the lecture grades of 299 students in a General Chemistry II course. The full model fit the data well and fit better than a restricted model that removed the path from intrinsic motivation to self-efficacy. Self-efficacy and mathematics preparation directly predicted lecture grades, and the model explained 22% of their variance, whereas intrinsic motivation was associated with achievement only indirectly, through its strong association with self-efficacy.
